title: Theme Detectives: Evidence That Holds Up
subject: ela
learningObjective: Identify a theme in a narrative and defend it with specific text evidence and reasoning.
successCriteria: I can state a theme as a message, not a one-word topic.
I can select two details that support the theme.
I can explain how each detail supports the message.
I can revise a theme claim when the evidence does not fit.
essentialQuestion: How can a reader prove that a theme is supported by the whole story?

quiz.question: Which statement is a theme rather than a topic?
choices: Courage
Friendship
People can become braver when they act even while afraid.
A character
quiz.correctAnswer: People can become braver when they act even while afraid.
quiz.explanation: A theme is a complete message about life or people, not just a topic word.

quiz.question: What makes a detail strong evidence for a theme?
choices: It is the first detail in the story.
It connects clearly to the message and can be explained.
It contains a difficult word.
It is the longest sentence.
quiz.correctAnswer: It connects clearly to the message and can be explained.
quiz.explanation: Evidence becomes useful when the reader explains how it supports the theme.

quiz.question: Which sentence best completes the reasoning? The character asks for help, so the story suggests that...
choices: helping others is always easy
people can solve every problem alone
asking for support can be a sign of strength
the character likes questions
quiz.correctAnswer: asking for support can be a sign of strength
quiz.explanation: The reasoning connects the action to a broader message.

quiz.question: Why is one isolated detail often weaker than a repeated pattern?
choices: A repeated pattern gives more support for an inference.
One detail is always incorrect.
Patterns make stories longer.
A reader should ignore single details.
quiz.correctAnswer: A repeated pattern gives more support for an inference.
quiz.explanation: Repeated choices, events, or images can show that a message matters across the story.

quiz.question: A claim says a story teaches that honesty builds trust, but every important character lies without consequences. What should the reader do?
choices: Keep the claim because it sounds positive.
Revise the claim because the evidence does not fit.
Add a topic word.
Ignore the character choices.
quiz.correctAnswer: Revise the claim because the evidence does not fit.
quiz.explanation: Strong readers test a claim against the whole pattern of evidence and revise when needed.

quiz.question: Which is the best way to cite a story detail in a theme explanation?
choices: Name a detail and explain how it supports the message.
Copy a random sentence with no explanation.
List the characters only.
State the theme again.
quiz.correctAnswer: Name a detail and explain how it supports the message.
quiz.explanation: A claim-evidence-reasoning response needs both the detail and the connection.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a topic and a theme?
choices: A topic is a message; a theme is a character.
A topic is a subject; a theme is a message about that subject.
They are exactly the same.
A topic only appears in nonfiction.
quiz.correctAnswer: A topic is a subject; a theme is a message about that subject.
quiz.explanation: The topic names what the story is about, while the theme explains what the story suggests.

quiz.question: Write one because sentence explaining how a character choice could support a theme.
quiz.correctAnswer: A response names a character choice, states a theme message, and connects them with because.
quiz.explanation: The explanation should make the evidence-to-message connection visible.

quiz.question: When a theme claim is too broad, what is the best revision move?
choices: Make the message more specific to the story evidence.
Add more unrelated characters.
Replace the message with one topic word.
Delete the evidence.
quiz.correctAnswer: Make the message more specific to the story evidence.
quiz.explanation: A precise claim is easier to defend with the details the story actually provides.

quiz.question: What should a reader do when a new scene does not fit the current theme claim?
choices: Pretend the scene is not important.
Use the new evidence to test and possibly revise the claim.
Choose the longest theme sentence.
Stop looking for patterns.
quiz.correctAnswer: Use the new evidence to test and possibly revise the claim.
quiz.explanation: Theme reasoning is an evidence-based process that stays open to revision.

knowledge: A theme is a message about life or people that a reader infers from repeated story evidence.
capability: Write a theme claim and connect two story details to it.
reasoning: Compare competing theme claims and reject one that the evidence cannot support.
retention: Retrieve the topic-versus-theme distinction after a delay.
transfer: Use the same evidence test on an unfamiliar short narrative or film scene.

visualSupports.title: The theme evidence board
visualSupports.description: A detective board connects repeated character choices to a message about people.
visualSupports.altText: Three story details connect by arrows to one theme message.

visualSupports.title: Claim to evidence to reasoning
visualSupports.description: A three-part chain shows that a detail is not proof until the reader explains the connection.
visualSupports.altText: A claim box points to an evidence box, which points to a reasoning box.

visualSupports.title: Topic or message?
visualSupports.description: Two cards compare courage as a topic with a complete message about courage.
visualSupports.altText: A topic word is contrasted with a full theme sentence.

phaseModules.title: Enter the evidence room
phaseModules.studentAction: Read a short scene, predict what message it might teach, and mark the detail that made you think that.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can name a first idea and the detail that sparked it.

phaseModules.title: Watch a reader build a claim
phaseModules.studentAction: Follow the visual chain from a repeated character choice to a theme message, then to the exact evidence.
phaseModules.successCheck: The model includes a message, a detail, and a because sentence.

phaseModules.title: Separate topic from theme
phaseModules.studentAction: Sort cards into topic, theme, evidence, or unsupported opinion. Rewrite one topic into a message.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can explain why a one-word topic is not yet a theme.

phaseModules.title: Build the evidence chain
phaseModules.studentAction: Choose two details from the scene and drag each to the claim it supports. Write one because sentence for each.
phaseModules.successCheck: Both details connect to the same message for a clear reason.

phaseModules.title: Cross-examine competing themes
phaseModules.studentAction: Compare two possible theme claims and use repeated details to decide which claim is stronger.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can reject a claim because the story does not provide enough evidence.

phaseModules.title: Defend a theme independently
phaseModules.studentAction: Write a theme claim, cite or paraphrase two details, and explain how each detail supports the message without tutor answers.
phaseModules.successCheck: A reader can follow my claim-evidence-reasoning chain.

phaseModules.title: Retrieve the reader test
phaseModules.studentAction: After a delay, explain the difference between topic and theme and name the three parts of a strong proof.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can retrieve the test without seeing the original board.

phaseModules.title: Use the test on a new scene
phaseModules.studentAction: Analyze an unfamiliar scene or film moment and defend a new theme with two details.
phaseModules.successCheck: The evidence method still works when the story changes.

phaseModules.title: Choose the next reading move
phaseModules.studentAction: If the claim is too broad, narrow it; if the evidence is weak, find a repeated detail; if the reasoning is missing, add a because sentence.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can name the exact part of my evidence chain that needs repair.

proofTasks.prompt: Define topic and theme and explain the difference.
Explain why one isolated detail is weaker than a repeated pattern.
Defend a theme in a new short narrative with two details and reasoning.
Complete a delayed topic-theme-evidence retrieval check.
Apply the evidence chain to a new scene, poem, or film moment.

feedbackRules.result: The response names a topic but not a message.
feedbackRules.hint: Finish the sentence: The story suggests that people should...
feedbackRules.action: Route to topic-versus-theme card sort and retry.

feedbackRules.result: The detail is relevant but the explanation does not connect it to the claim.
feedbackRules.hint: Add: This supports my theme because...

feedbackRules.result: One moment is treated as proof of the whole story.
feedbackRules.hint: Look for a repeated choice, consequence, or change.

reteachPaths.trigger: Theme claim or evidence chain is incomplete.
reteachPaths.action: Use a short scene, highlight repeated choices, and complete one claim-because-detail frame before returning to the full proof.

prerequisiteRepairPaths.trigger: The learner cannot identify a character change or sequence of events.
prerequisiteRepairPaths.action: Repair event sequencing and character-change notes with a three-panel story map.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner independently defends a theme with relevant evidence.
challengePaths.action: Compare two stories with a related theme and explain how each author develops the message differently.

commonMisunderstandings: A topic word is the same as a theme.
Any detail from the story proves any theme.
A theme must be a universal rule or moral.
parentTeacherNotes: Require students to explain the evidence link. A correct theme with weak reasoning is developing, not transferable mastery.
accessibilityNotes: Provide a text-to-speech version and a text-only evidence board.
Allow typed, spoken, or recorded claim-evidence-reasoning responses.
Use labels and patterns in addition to color.
